L104: Gregory L. Possehl spent parts of his academic life on archaeological digs in South
L105: Asia, but he also paid attention to the West Philadelphia neighborhood of the University
L106: of Pennsylvania Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology.
L107: "One of the roles the University Museum plays is as a doorway for our neighbors to see
L108: what goes on at the University of Pennsylvania," Dr. Possehl explained in a 1985
L109: Inquirer interview.
L110: Speaking of a Penn exhibit on the history of Buddhism meant in part to attract
L111: nonacademics, he noted: "This is an educational display that will be pretty, too, by the
L112: way. We don't mind being beautiful as long as we have our message."
L113: Dr. Possehl, 70, associate director of the University Museum from 1981 to 1992 and
L114: chairman of Penn's department of anthropology from 1994 to 2001, died of respiratory
L115: failure Saturday, Oct. 8, at Boston Medical Center.
L116: "Dr. Possehl was a leading expert on the rise of the Indus civilization in India and
L117: Pakistan," Penn biographical notes state.
L118: That ancient Indus society, researched at more than 2,000 archaeological sites along
L119: the Indus and Sarasvati Rivers, existed from 4300 to 1500 B.C.
L120: To help authenticate his studies, Dr. Possehl wrote on his website, he spent nine
L121: seasons on excavations of ancient sites in the Indian state of Gujarat.
L122: AltaMira Press published his book, The Indus Civilization: A Contemporary Perspective.
L123: A 2004 Penn announcement reported that the work had been named Outstanding
L124: Academic Book for 2003 by Choice magazine, which Penn described as "the key
L125: publication for academic librarians across the nation selecting books for collections."
L126: He had published papers in several scholarly journals.
L127: Dr. Possehl went far afield to share his enthusiasms with nonacademic audiences.
L128: He was one of three lecturers on a 1981 trip to India sponsored by the Women's
L129: Committee of the Penn Museum and the Friends of the Philadelphia Museum of Art.
L130: In a 1981 Inquirer Sunday magazine story reporting on the trip, Dr. Possehl told the
L131: reporter accompanying the lecturers that a certain ficus tree is considered sacred by
L132: Hindus because of its size.
L133: "Greg, who himself is quite large at 6-3, is also regarded as special because of his
L134: size," the reporter wrote. "When he strides through a village, people touch him for luck."
L135: Born in Tacoma, Wash., he earned a bachelor's degree in 1964 and a master's in 1967,
L136: both at the University of Washington, and a doctorate at the University of Chicago in
L137: 1974, all in anthropology.

L142: Gregory Possehl
L143: Gregory Louis Possehl (July 21, 1941 October 8, 2011) was a Professor Emeritus of
L144: Anthropology at the University of Pennsylvania and curator of the Asian Collections at
L145: the University of Pennsylvania Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology.
L146: [1]
L147: He has
L148: been involved in excavations of the Indus Valley Civilization in India and Pakistan since
L149: 1964, and is an author of many books and articles on the Indus Civilization and related
L150: topics. He received his BA in Anthropology from the University of Washington in 1964,
L151: his MA in Anthropology from the University of Washington in 1967, and his PhD in
L152: Anthropology from the University of Chicago in 1974. He has conducted major
L153: excavations in Gujarat (Rojdi, Babar Kot and Oriyo Timbo), Rajasthan (Gilund), and in
L154: January 2007, began an excavation at the UNESCO World Heritage site of Bat in the
L155: Sultanate of Oman.
L156: [2]
L157: He is an exponent of the view that the culture of the Vedic period is a direct successor
L158: of the Indus Valley Civilization. In his book Ancient Cities of the Indus he writes that "the
L159: first point to be emphasized is that the problem seems not to be best stated as the "end"
L160: of a civilization, at least in the sense of a tradition, since there are abundant signs of
L161: cultural continuity in Sindh, Gujarat, the Punjab and adjacent areas of the North India."
